correctness.rationale: For equal-sum vectors, a common 3-multiset exists iff I(x,y)>=3. Heavy vectors (some component>=3) have pairwise-disjoint nonempty heavy-coordinate sets, hence at most q. Any two light vectors satisfy I>=2n-2q>=4 for n>=q+2, hence at most one light; no light exists for n>=2q+1. q pure constant vectors, plus one 1/2-valued vector when n<=2q, attain both bounds. Equality forces all q heavy-coordinate sets to be singleton and distinct. Two explicit 1/2-valued boundary vectors at n=q+1 give q+2 total. Exact independent clique checks passed for 18 q,n pairs and construction checks for 897 pairs; neither finite test substitutes for the complete proof.

originality.rationale: The closest full primary text, arXiv:2601.05636v2, Section 4.4 Proposition 12, proves only S_q(n,n-3)<=q+binom(q,2) in the same regime. The new exact all-q two-regime theorem and forced unique-heavy-coordinate feature are not implied by that upper bound or by the already known q=2,3,4 special cases. Both primary and published-result searches were checked for the equivalent l1/simplex statements. This is best-knowledge priority, not a claim of independent certification.
residual_risks: An unindexed or unpublished earlier proof could already provide the q-uniform theorem.
The q=2,3,4 special cases are prior coverage; novelty applies only to the uniform structural theorem.
No independent mathematical or priority audit has been performed.

value.rationale: A current paper leaves the natural three-surviving-symbol, high-deletion regime with a general bound quadratic in q. The theorem determines the exact optimum for every alphabet and all n>=q+2, identifies the sharp n=2q+1 transition and the sharp starting boundary, and gives necessary structural restrictions for every optimizer. E.g. q=5,n=7 improves published upper bound 15 to exact value 6, and all n>=11 have exact value 5. It is an infinite, naturally parameterized extremal coding problem rather than an arbitrary instance or restated special case.
